posts.quote: THE JANITOR SPRINKLED RED SWEEPING COMPOUND ON EVERY MESS, AND ONE SMELL TAKES ME STRAIGHT BACK TO THIRD GRADE.
posts.caption: Somebody threw up in the hallway, and within two minutes a man with a wide push broom appeared out of nowhere. He shook a little red-brown powder out of a bucket onto the spot like he was seasoning a roast. Nobody in the class got to look closer than the doorway. The stuff smelled of sawdust, kerosene, and something nobody could name, and it was gone by lunch. Teachers never had to say a word. The janitor handled the worst moment of the day and went right back to his boiler room without anyone thanking him.
posts.first: Our janitor was Mr. Pruitt, and he kept a ring of keys on his belt as big as a dinner plate. He fixed my broken desk lid with a nail he pulled out of his pocket. I never heard him say more than ten words in a row, and every one was useful.

posts.quote: Grandma kept plastic on the good sofa, and every July you left a little of yourself behind.
posts.first: Nobody ever sat on that sofa except the preacher and the insurance man. It crackled when you moved and kept the cushions looking brand new for thirty years. My cousin and I got caught bouncing on it once and never lived it down.

posts.character: Cars and driving culture (the trunk kit)
posts.quote: THE TRUNK OF DAD'S CAR HELD A JACK, A BLANKET, A FLASHLIGHT, AND A CAN OF OIL, JUST IN CASE.
posts.caption: Before any long drive, Dad popped the trunk and counted everything out loud like a pilot. A jack, a lug wrench, a wool blanket with a moth hole in one corner, a flashlight that worked about half the time, and a quart of oil. There was a coil of rope in there too, though nobody ever learned why. We broke down twice in ten years, and both times he had exactly what the moment needed. Roadside help was a man named Earl at the filling station, and you walked to find him. So you carried what you might need and hoped the trunk would be enough.
posts.first: Our trunk always smelled like rubber and old canvas. I rode in the back seat with a pillow, listening to the spare tire thump every time we hit a pothole. Dad checked that trunk before every trip, and I never saw him skip it.

posts.quote: THE MIMEOGRAPH / PURPLE INK, A HAND CRANK, AND A SHEET STILL DAMP FROM THE MACHINE
posts.caption: The teacher passed back the quiz and every head in the room dipped at once. The page was still damp and smelled sweet and sharp, like nothing else on earth. You held it up to your face for one second before you read the first question. Mimeographed sheets came off the machine in faded purple, and the last few copies were always too light to read. The teacher cranked the handle in the workroom at the end of the hall, and sometimes you caught the smell in the corridor before you saw the paper. Nobody ever explained why we all did it. We just did.
posts.first: Our school secretary ran the mimeograph, and she wore a smock so the ink wouldn't get on her good blouse. Her fingertips were purple most of the year. I still think of her when I smell a fresh page.

posts.quote: WHEN A FUNERAL WENT BY, EVERY CAR PULLED OVER, AND EVERY MAN TOOK OFF HIS HAT.
posts.caption: The procession came slowly down Main Street with its headlights on in broad daylight. A man on the corner stopped in the middle of a sentence and took off his hat. The cars along the curb pulled over and sat still with their engines off. Even the delivery truck waited, and the driver stood beside it with his head down. None of them knew who had died, and nobody asked. It lasted about three minutes, and then the street started up again as if nothing had happened.
posts.first: My father pulled our car over for every funeral we ever passed, even when we were running late. He would sit with both hands on the wheel and not say a word. I learned more from those three minutes than from a lot of lessons.

posts.quote: THE JELLY JAR GLASSES HAD CARTOONS ON THEM, AND EVERY KID FOUGHT FOR THE GOOD ONE.
posts.caption: Our drinking glasses started out as jelly. Mom saved every empty jar, ran it through hot water until the label floated off, and set it in the cupboard with the others. The ones with the painted cartoon figures on the side were the prize, and there were only four of them. Every supper somebody got to the cupboard first and the rest of us sulked. By the time the paint wore off, the glasses had been through about ten thousand dishwashings and not one cracked. A glass that cost nothing and lasted forever suited our house fine.
posts.first: I still have one of those glasses, with the figure worn down to a faint outline. It sits in my kitchen window with a pencil in it. Nobody has ever been allowed to drink from it since we left the old house.

posts.quote: Nobody told you the rule, but the last one to the supper table washed the dishes.
posts.first: Dad was always last, because he came in from the shed smelling of oil. He washed every night anyway and never complained. Mom dried, and we kids put away.

posts.character: Crafts and homemaking (the flour sack shirts)
posts.quote: MOM SEWED OUR SUMMER SHIRTS FROM FLOUR SACKS, AND SHE PICKED THE FLOUR BY THE PATTERN.
posts.caption: At the feed store, Mom stood in front of the flour sacks for a long time, turning each one to see the print. She wasn't choosing flour. She was choosing shirts, and a good yellow check could outfit two boys by June. At home she washed the sacks, ironed out the creases, and laid the pattern pieces right on the kitchen table. The sewing machine ran until supper. Every boy on our road wore a shirt that began as somebody's twenty-five pounds of flour, and nobody thought it odd. We only wondered who got the blue ones.
posts.first: My brother and I wore matching shirts for one whole summer. Mine had a little ink mark on the back where the brand name was, and no amount of washing took it out. Mom said it was a good luck stamp.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the watch repairman)
posts.quote: THE WATCH REPAIR SHOP / A LOUPE, A TRAY OF TINY SCREWS, AND A STEADY HAND
posts.caption: The repairman sat at a bench in the front window with a little glass screwed into his eye. He worked on a watch the way a surgeon works, with tweezers and a lamp and absolutely no talking. Customers stood at the counter and waited quietly because interrupting felt wrong. Behind him, a hundred clocks ticked slightly out of step. When he looked up and said, "Tuesday," it meant Tuesday. Your grandfather's watch came back running, and the bill was always smaller than you feared.
posts.first: My dad's wristwatch stopped the day he came home from the service, and the shop on Elm Street got it going again. He wore it for thirty-one years. It was never fixed twice.

posts.character: Entertainment (the one television on the block)
posts.quote: THE ONLY TELEVISION ON OUR STREET BELONGED TO THE JOHNSONS, AND THE WHOLE BLOCK SHOWED UP FOR THE WORLD SERIES.
posts.caption: By the second inning the Johnsons' living room held eleven grown-ups and nine children, and not one chair was left. Kids sat cross-legged on the rug inches from the screen while the men stood in the doorway with their arms folded. The picture was small and gray, and somebody always had to adjust the rabbit ears. Mrs. Johnson came around with a tray of lemonade and never once asked anyone to leave. When the last out was made, the whole room cheered like it was their own team. We walked home in the dark, still talking about it, and the Johnsons turned the set off and began sweeping up.
posts.first: Mr. Johnson let me turn the knob once, in the seventh inning, and I thought I was the most important boy in town. The picture rolled for a moment and every man in the room groaned. I handed the knob back politely.
